sections.h2: How New Jersey sets property tax
sections.html:
Value drives the tax, and local budgets turn that value into a bill. Each parcel is measured against true value, meaning the price a willing buyer and a willing seller would agree on in an open sale, fixed on one statutory snapshot date in the autumn before the tax year. All 21 counties assess at the full 100 percent of that value.

Equalization compares the 566 taxing districts so that county government and shared school costs are split fairly between towns. A municipality finds its general rate by dividing the amount its budget must raise by the combined assessed value of everything taxable inside its borders. Your bill is that rate times your assessment, and the State itself receives none of the money.

Because the amount comes out of county, municipal and school budgets, you cannot contest the tax as such. You can only contest the assessment underneath it.

Four payments fall due across the year: Feb. 1, May 1, Aug. 1 and Nov. 1. A missed installment starts accruing interest. Unpaid tax on real estate is a continuous lien, so the debt follows the house into any sale.

A late balance may be charged up to 8 percent annually on its first $1,500 and up to 18 percent on whatever exceeds that figure. When a town's overdue total tops $10,000 at fiscal year end, it may add a further penalty of up to 6 percent. Municipalities collect these amounts, so call the tax collector for a dated payoff instead of estimating from a bill.

The route runs through your County Board of Taxation, and the calendar is strict. The filing cutoff is April 1 each year, or 45 days after assessment notices are mailed in bulk. A town that has just finished a revaluation or reassessment moves the cutoff to May 1. Three counties, Burlington, Gloucester and Monmouth, run a different assessment calendar, and their cutoff is January 15.

You carry the burden of proof, and the board weighs true market value against the taxable assessment. Evidence should predate the October 1 assessment date. A strong petition usually includes:

  • three to five sales of similar homes, attached when you file
  • photographs of your home and of each comparable
  • copies of those comparables delivered to both the assessor and the board a week or more before the hearing
  • an income statement, if the property is commercial

Hearings generally take place within three months of the filing cutoff, and the board must decide within that same window. Adjournments are rarely granted. If you skip the hearing, the case can end for lack of prosecution, and that closes the door to the Tax Court. The assessments of neighboring properties do not count as proof, so lean on actual sales.

To show an assessment is excessive or discriminatory, you must prove it misses the True Market Value Standard or the Common Level Range Standard. The range extends 15 percent above and below the Director's Ratio, the average assessed-to-true-value percentage the State certifies for each taxing district.

If your property's ratio lands above the range, the board resets taxable value by multiplying true value by the district's average ratio. A win also brings the Freeze Act into play: the new figure stays put for that year and the following two, unless a revaluation or an added assessment intervenes or you appeal again.

ANCHOR is the largest, and it pays by income band. Using 2025 income, homeowners at or below $150,000 get $1,500, while those between $150,001 and $250,000 get $1,000. Renters receive $450, or $700 if they were 65 or older by the end of 2025. Checks go out on a rolling schedule beginning September 15, typically within 90 days of the application. All relief combined cannot exceed the property tax actually paid on the main home.

Senior Freeze repays seniors and disabled residents for tax increases on their main home, measured from a base year, and the Stay NJ credit rides on the same combined form. Senior citizen, disabled person and veteran deductions also count toward the cap. Check the Division of Taxation's relief page when a new application round opens.

sections.h2: Does the owner lose the house at a tax sale?
sections.html:
No, not at the auction. The sale puts a lien up for bid, and the title stays with the owner. Every municipality with delinquent taxes or charges must hold at least one sale yearly. Bidders compete by lowering the interest rate they will accept, starting from 18 percent. When bids reach one percent, they switch to offering a premium.

You can redeem the certificate by paying the amount owed plus a redemption penalty of 2, 4 or 6 percent, set by the certificate's size. Foreclosure is possible only after two years: the certificate holder may then sue in Superior Court, and a successful suit moves the deed to the holder. Learn your town's sale schedule from the collector well ahead of time.

Dates and limits to check against a tax bill or notice

Start with the tax collector. Request a written payoff that lists current installments, interest and any other municipal charges, and ask whether a tax sale is on the calendar. Hand that figure to the title agent so the amount is settled out of the sale. Before you agree to a closing date, line up these items:

  • the payoff letter, dated close to the settlement day
  • the date of the next tax sale, if the property is delinquent
  • proof of any ANCHOR, Senior Freeze or deduction benefit already received
  • the status of any open assessment appeal, which may produce a refund or a changed bill

At closing, the title agent pays the collector from your proceeds and the lien comes off the house. A payoff dated close to settlement matters because interest keeps running until the day the money arrives. A cash sale skips the buyer's mortgage underwriting, so the closing date is easier to fix once you know the payoff and any sale date.

faqs.q: Can I appeal the tax bill itself in New Jersey?
faqs.a: No. Only the assessment can be contested. The amount owed comes from local budgets, so the petition goes to the county board, aimed at the value, before the cutoff that applies where you live.

faqs.q: When must a New Jersey assessment petition be filed?
faqs.a: By April 1 in most places, or within 45 days of the bulk mailing of notices. Revaluation towns use May 1. Burlington, Gloucester and Monmouth Counties use January 15.

faqs.q: What does ANCHOR pay a New Jersey homeowner?
faqs.a: It pays $1,500 to homeowners with 2025 income of $150,000 or less and $1,000 to those earning $150,001 to $250,000. Above that, a homeowner does not qualify.

faqs.q: How much interest builds on a late payment?
faqs.a: Up to 8 percent on the first $1,500 and up to 18 percent on the rest. A town may also add up to 6 percent when overdue taxes pass $10,000 at fiscal year end.

faqs.q: Can New Jersey take a home over delinquent taxes?
faqs.a: Not directly. The town auctions a lien certificate, and the holder cannot begin a Superior Court foreclosure until two years pass. Paying the certificate off, with the added penalty, ends the process.
